# Why Stream Processing? Why Another Engine? {#sec-why-streaming}

::: {.callout-note title="Status: complete first draft"}
:::

The history of database systems is, in a coarse approximation, a history
of attempts to deal with data that does not fit. Data that does not fit
in main memory motivated the buffer manager. Data that does not fit on
one disk motivated partitioning. Data that does not fit in one
transaction motivated isolation levels. And data that does not fit
inside a query — that *arrives*, continuously, while the query runs —
motivated stream processing.

This is a book about a particular stream processing engine. Before we
open it up, though, we should be honest about why such engines exist,
why we keep building new ones, and why NebulaStream is worth a book of
its own.

---

## 1.1 A short history of streaming engines {#sec-streaming-history}

The first generation of streaming systems were academic. Aurora (2003),
Borealis (2005) and TelegraphCQ (2003) established that a continuous
query — a query that runs forever, producing a continuous answer — was
a coherent mathematical object, not just a hack on top of a relational
DBMS. They taught us about windowing, watermarks, and what it meant
for a query to "complete" without ever stopping.

The second generation went into production. Apache Storm (2011),
later Apache Flink (2015), Apache Spark Streaming (2013) and Kafka
Streams (2016) brought streaming to industry. They solved the
operational problems the academic systems left open — checkpointing,
exactly-once processing, scaling to thousands of nodes, integration
with the Hadoop and Kafka ecosystems. But they did so under a particular
set of assumptions: data lived in the cloud, infrastructure was
elastic, latency budgets were measured in seconds, and the engine was
written in a JVM language because the surrounding ecosystem was JVM.

The third generation is happening now, and is more diffuse. Materialize
(2019) showed that incremental view maintenance could be a streaming
abstraction in its own right. Arroyo and RisingWave brought SQL-first
streaming with column-oriented internals. ClickHouse and Pinot blurred
the line between streaming and OLAP. Hyper, Umbra and Velox demonstrated
that JIT-compiled query execution could be twenty times faster than
interpreted execution. None of these systems is "the" streaming engine;
each embodies a different bet about what stream processing should look
like in 2025.

NebulaStream is one of those bets. It is an academic project — joint
between BIFOLD, the DIMA Group at TU Berlin and the DFKI IAM Group —
which means it is both freer to experiment than a production system
and more accountable to ideas than to revenue. Its bet is that the
*shape of computation* is changing: data is no longer being produced
inside data centres and processed in data centres. It is being produced
at the edge — in factories, in vehicles, in medical devices, in
agriculture — and the network between the edge and the cloud is the
expensive part. A streaming engine that takes that seriously will look
different from one that does not.

---

## 1.2 What NebulaStream optimises for {#sec-nes-vision}

The README opens with an unusually clear thesis statement. We will
quote it in full because it sets up everything that follows in the
book:

> NebulaStream is an end-to-end data-management system for cloud-edge-sensor
> deployments. The platform combines ease of use, extensibility, and
> efficiency to let teams focus on business logic while the engine
> optimizes the data path.
>
> We advance this vision through five core technologies:
>
> - **Heterogeneous Hardware Support** — Targets diverse CPU
>   architectures and accelerators such as GPUs and TPUs.
> - **Code Generation** — Compiles every query to efficient native
>   code for low latency and energy usage.
> - **In-Network Processing** — Pushes operators toward data sources
>   to reduce network traffic.
> - **Adaptive Resource Management** — Reacts to topology or workload
>   changes without interrupting queries.

Each of these gets at least one chapter in the book. Two need a brief
preview here, because they shape the engine's design from the very
top.

**Code generation everywhere.** NebulaStream does not interpret a query
plan. It compiles the query plan into native machine code, every time,
through a tracing-JIT framework called Nautilus that lowers to MLIR
and ultimately to LLVM IR. We will see this in detail in
@sec-nautilus-codegen. The choice has consequences for almost every
other design decision: the operator interface looks more like a
producer/consumer protocol than a class hierarchy, intermediate data
structures are designed for the JIT (`HashMap`, `PagedVector`) rather
than the C++ standard library, and the boundary between "query plan"
and "executable" is a compile step that can take milliseconds and
returns a function pointer. If you have only ever written queries
against an interpreter-based engine, this is the single largest
mental shift the book will ask you to make.

**Cloud-edge-sensor as a first-class deployment target.** Almost every
streaming engine in production today was designed for the cloud and
then asked to run at the edge. The result tends to be a JVM heap on a
Raspberry Pi, which is exactly as awkward as it sounds. NebulaStream
inverts the question: the edge is the constraint, the cloud is the
luxury. C++23, no garbage collector, every byte accounted for. This
shows up in the data model (Chapter 3), where the unit of inter-operator
data flow is a fixed-size buffer with explicit reference counting, and
in the buffer manager (Chapter 4), where pre-allocated pools are the
default rather than dynamic allocation. We will see throughout the
book how these foundations propagate up the stack.

The other three technologies — heterogeneous hardware, in-network
processing, adaptive resource management — are partially implemented
and partially aspirational. We will be honest about which parts of
the vision are running today and which are research roadmap. The
distribution story in particular has moved fast: the coordinator
and inter-worker communication that earlier drafts of this book
described as "research roadmap" have landed on `origin/main` since
those drafts were written. Chapter 19 covers what shipped and
what is still in flight.

---

## 1.3 Why a book on this engine? {#sec-why-this-book}

There is no shortage of textbooks on databases. Garcia-Molina, Ullman
and Widom's *Database Systems: The Complete Book* is the canonical
undergraduate text on the relational model, SQL, B-trees, transaction
processing, and the canonical query optimiser. Petrov's *Database
Internals* takes the reader on a curated tour of how distributed data
systems are actually built — storage engines, consensus, replication.
Kleppmann's *Designing Data-Intensive Applications* sits one level
above: not "how is X implemented" but "how should I think about X."
Akidau, Chernyak and Lax's *Streaming Systems* covers the conceptual
landscape of stream processing — windowing, triggers, accumulation
modes — at a level any practitioner should have in working memory.

Each of these books leaves the same gap. None of them takes a single
*specimen* — a single, concrete, modern stream processing engine — and
walks the reader through it end to end. The closest thing is
Lions's *Commentary on UNIX 6th Edition*, a book written in 1976 that
is still in print, because nothing else does for a kernel what Lions
did. We need a Lions's commentary on a stream engine.

NebulaStream is a good specimen for that purpose, for several reasons.

It is **small enough to fit in a book**: about 876 source files across
sixteen modules, mostly C++. Production engines like Flink (about
ten times larger) would need three books to cover at this fidelity.

It is **modern enough to be interesting**: code-generation, MLIR,
plugin registries, C++20 concepts, statically-linked plugin systems.
Every chapter has something a reader who knows a different engine
will not have seen before.

It is **documented well enough to be tractable**: NebulaStream's
in-tree `docs/design/` and `docs/technical/` directories contain
substantive design documents that explain *why* a thing works the
way it does, not just *how*. We will lift heavily from them, with
attribution, because the team has already done the work of writing
down the rationale.

And it is **academic enough to be honest about what does not work**:
production engines bury their workarounds in proprietary commits and
internal Slack messages. A research engine can — and does — leave
its scars on the surface. Chapter 15's "the design document says
continuation, but the live code uses an unbounded queue" is a
microcosm of the kind of intellectual honesty this book is interested
in.

---

## 1.4 Who is this book for? {#sec-audience}

Three audiences in roughly decreasing priority:

**Graduate students in systems.** This book sits at the same
"mezzanine" level as Garcia-Molina/Ullman/Widom: between an
undergraduate algorithms class and a primary research paper. We
assume you can read C++, that you have seen relational algebra,
that you know what a watermark is in principle. We do not assume you
have built a database. The exercises are designed for self-study and
for use in a graduate seminar — none require a problem set in the
traditional sense; all point at real tests inside the engine and ask
you to run them, observe, and explain.

**Engineers building dataflow systems.** If you are building Flink
operators, Materialize sources, or your own bespoke streaming
infrastructure, this book is a tour of one set of choices that you
might compare your own choices against. Each chapter ends with a
"Real-system reference" sidebar that places NebulaStream's design
next to Flink's, Spark's, or Materialize's. The point is not to claim
NebulaStream is better. The point is to make the design space
visible.

**NebulaStream maintainers and contributors.** A book by definition
goes stale; a book pinned to a specific commit goes stale fast. But a
book that records the *reasoning* behind a system's design is a thing
the engineers who built that system can hand to a new contributor on
their first day. If you are about to send your first PR to
NebulaStream, this book is the long form of "go read the design
docs" — distilled, cross-referenced, and assembled into a coherent
narrative.

What this book is **not**: a user manual. We will not teach you the
SQL you need to express a windowed top-K. The official documentation
will. We will use SQL extensively as a vehicle for explaining what
the engine does next, but we will not stop to explain what `GROUP
BY` means.

---

## 1.5 What the book does not cover {#sec-non-goals-book}

Three deliberate omissions, each motivated.

**Comparative survey.** We compare to Flink, Spark, Materialize,
Hyper and Arroyo *only* when a comparison illuminates a NebulaStream
design choice, and *only* in clearly-marked sidebars of half a page
or less. If you want a comparative survey of stream processing
engines, Akidau, Chernyak and Lax wrote it.

**Distributed systems theory.** We assume you have at least a
working knowledge of leader election, linearisability, network
partitions and CAP. Where NebulaStream's design depends on a
specific theoretical result, we cite the paper. We do not re-derive
results that other books — Petrov in particular — have already
covered in depth.

**Anything outside the engine itself.** The Kubernetes operator,
the deployment scripts, the cloud integration, the observability
stack — all useful, none in this book. The line we have drawn is:
if it is not under `/Users/zeuchste/git/nebulastream/`, it is not in
scope.

## 1.6 Reading order {#sec-dependencies}

The book has 22 chapters in five parts. Most readers will want to
read Part I (Foundations) in order; thereafter, the chapters are
mostly independent. The hard dependencies are:

![Reading-order dependencies between the book's five parts. Solid arrows are hard prerequisites; the dashed arrow from Part II to Part V is a soft dependency (Part V's Testing chapter cross-references Part II's data model).](../figures/tikz/ch01-dependencies.svg){#fig-deps width=100%}

If you are interested in code generation, jump to Chapter 12 after
Part I. If you are interested in scheduling, jump to Chapter 15.
If you are interested in plugins and how a third party adds a new
source, Chapter 13 is largely self-contained.

---

## Summary {#sec-ch1-summary}

NebulaStream is a third-generation streaming engine — academic,
C++23-native, JIT-compiled, designed from the start for the cloud-
edge-sensor spectrum rather than retrofitted to it. It is small
enough to dissect in one book, modern enough to be interesting, and
documented well enough to be tractable. The book uses NebulaStream
as a single specimen the way an OS textbook uses xv6 or MINIX: not
because it is the best engine, but because seeing one engine end to
end is more instructive than seeing five engines half-way each.

The remaining 21 chapters fill in the steps between SQL text and
running native code, with one chapter per major concern. Chapter 2,
next, gives the whirlwind tour: a single query, traced through every
module, in about 35 pages.

---

## Reading exercises {#sec-ch1-exercises}

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 1.1: orient yourself in the repo"}
Locate the NebulaStream repository, then run:

```shell
ls /Users/zeuchste/git/nebulastream/ | grep '^nes-'
```

You should see sixteen `nes-*` directories. Each module has a
one- or two-line statement of purpose in `CLAUDE.md`. Match each
module to the part of the book that covers it (this chapter's
@sec-dependencies diagram is the index).
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 1.2: find the design documents"}
Run:

```shell
ls /Users/zeuchste/git/nebulastream/docs/design/
```

You should see at least six dated `.md` files. These are the
in-tree design documents the book cites repeatedly. Pick one and
read its first page. What problem is it solving? Is the solution
the one currently in the code, or has the design evolved? (Chapter
15 walks through one example of design-doc-vs-code drift; you may
spot more.)
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 1.3: build it"}
Follow the README's "Build & Tooling" section to compile NebulaStream.
The Nix path (`nix run .#clion-setup`) is fastest if you have Nix;
otherwise the Docker development image is the next-best option. Once
you have a `cmake-build-debug/` directory, run:

```shell
ctest --test-dir cmake-build-debug -j --output-on-failure
```

You should see hundreds of unit tests pass. We will be re-running
specific tests throughout the book; this exercise just establishes
that the engine builds for you.
:::
